newsitem.title: BULGARIA: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT STARTS WORK ON CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: NEW BULGARIAN PRESIDENT STARTS WORK ON CRISIS.

text.p: New president Petar Stoyanov starts work on Thursday on unravelling Bulgaria's political and economic crisis, with Socialists impatient to form a cabinet threatening protests which could lead to fresh violence.

Stoyanov, who took office in a colourful religious and military ceremony on Wednesday, will meet leaders of the Socialists and the opposition to seek a way out of political deadlock blocking an urgently needed economic crisis programme.

After 16 days of opposition rallies for quick elections and against a new Socialist government, the ex-communist ruling party on Wednesday approved potentially explosive counter-protests by its supporters around the country.

"It will be a funny picture to see red grannies rallying against Bulgarian students," said Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), referring to the Socialists' mainly elderly supporters.
"When this is over, the BSP will be history," he told the daily opposition rally, which gathered about 18,000 people.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but in the meantime they want to form a new cabinet following prime minister Zhan Videnov's resignation last December 21. The UDF wants elections in March.
Students staged a symbolic funeral for the Socialists at the mausoleum of Bulgarian communist hero Georgi Dimitrov.
Weeping women prostrated themselves on a coffin draped with a red communist flag as a band played funeral marches.
One banner bore tables showing the lev's decline against the dollar to make a professor's monthly salary worth the equivalent of $35.

Valery Radev, regional party leader from the mining town of Bobov Dol, near Sofia, told reporters counter-protests could start immediately and would continue until the new president gave the Socialists a mandate to form a government.
Counter-rallies by supporters of neighbouring Serbia's Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on December 24 led to clashes between demonstrators and riot police.
Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket in November, took over command of the army from outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev at a military parade outside the presidency.
He then received the blessing of the Orthodox church in the first religious ceremony for a new head of state since Boris III became king in October 1918.
The president cancelled the usual champagne reception as inappropriate at a time when hundreds of thousands of Bulgarians are hungry.

Stoyanov, a lawyer who specialises in divorce cases, backed opposition calls for early elections at his swearing-in ceremony last Sunday in the parliament, which was besieged and ransacked by demonstrators on January 10.

Under its post-communist constitution, Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic whose president is a mainly ceremonial figure, but one of his tasks is to ask the prime minister nominated by the largest parliamentary group to form a government.
Zhelev has refused to ask the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) to form a government in the present explosive atmosphere, but Stoyanov has said he is prepared to do so as the constitution requires.
Sokolov appeared to confirm fears that this might only heighten tension in the Balkan country of 8.4 million people.

"At our meeting with the president we shall suggest that he should give a mandate to the Socialists as soon as possible because we are ready for a general strike and we are going to sweep them out once and for all," he said.
Trade unions have warned of a general strike, but warning strikes have not won universal support. -- Sofia Newsroom, (++359-2) 981 8569; 981 4145
